To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) MVCC is a viable option for in-memory DBMSs; (2) the performance of MVCC depends heavily on the concurrency control protocol and the garbage collection scheme; (3) the version storage scheme is less critical; and (4) the index management scheme is not critical.
(1) MVCC is not a good choice in multi-core, in-memory settings.

In summary, our research is concerned with
the following questions: 1) How does multi-version concurrency control perform in a multi-core, in-memory setting?
the following questions: (1) What are the key bottlenecks of MVCC in modern hardware?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
MVCC is not suitable for multi-threaded in-memory databases.

(1) a multi-version concurrency control scheme can be implemented in a way that is scalable to modern hardware; and (2) the design of such a scheme is not trivial and should be based on an extensive empirical study of the underlying hardware and workloads.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
MVCC can scale well with increasing parallelism and transaction rates.
the MVCC scheme can be made to scale to a large number of cores and threads, provided the design decisions are made with care.
MVCC is not a panacea for multi-core and inmemory systems.
The main takeaway from our work is that

, when there are multiple threads running in parallel on a modern multi-core machine, a simple protocol such as timestamp ordering is the best concurrency control protocol, and a simple version storage scheme such as a hash map is the best way to store versions in an in-memory setting.
MVCC can scale well in multi-core, in-memory settings.
MVCC can be a scalable and performant transaction management scheme when the DBMS is optimized for modern hardware.
